status: PROPOSAL - research data only. This file is NOT authoritative simulation state and NOT renderer presentation data. It does not finalise a runtime schema. Canonical settlement/location identities (RFC 4122 UUIDv5, ADR-0009) are minted only by the atlas pipeline at integration time; the proposedId values here are research handles, not canonical IDs.
subject: R-16 historical settlement roster, ninth batch (batch 9)
envelopeRegions: 4 - Britain & Ireland (mid ~8); 5 - Germania, Alps & inner Europe (mid ~12)
batchScope: Iron Age Britain and Ireland (hillforts, a coastal emporion and royal/ceremonial sites) and the Celtic La Tene zone of the Alps, Bohemia, Moravia and the Carpathian basin together with the Germania borderland; the most under-attested parts of the 278 BCE envelope.
coordinateConvention: WGS84 decimal degrees, approximate representative points for the ancient site (not the modern town unless noted). Precision does not imply archaeological accuracy and is not a surveyed building location. In Britain and Ireland many sites are known only archaeologically and carry no ancient place-name in any text.
idScheme: proposedId = r16-bri-<slug> for Britain & Ireland (envelope region 4) or r16-grm-<slug> for Germania, Alps & inner Europe (envelope region 5); the slug (key) is region-scoped to avoid homonyms. Stable, human-readable, non-canonical.
methodNote: Records are compiled from independent evidence (archaeological excavation, primary literary/administrative sources and the Pleiades gazetteer for coordinates). Game/mod faction names are discovery leads only and never authorities. Every coordinate is a representative point with an explicit location confidence; where only a broad location is known the coordinate is coarse or null. Political authority is recorded only where supported; otherwise it is left unclaimed. For regions 4 and 5 the policy is to record fewer, well-evidenced sites and to leave doubt explicit rather than pad the roster with invented settlements or names.
sourceAuditNote: Pleiades gazetteer identifiers are recorded only as 'to be confirmed', never asserted: automated access to pleiades.stoa.org was blocked by the site's anti-scraping protection during this pass, so no Pleiades id has been verified. Coordinates are approximate representative points, not surveyed locations. For Britain and Ireland the only near-contemporary literary source is Pytheas of Massalia (c. 325 BCE), which survives only through later writers (Strabo, Diodorus); Caesar is mid-1st c. BCE, Tacitus late 1st/early 2nd c. CE, and Ptolemy's geography 2nd c. CE, so the ancient place-names and ethnonyms available for these islands are later geography and must never be treated as a 278 contemporary snapshot. In the Celtic/Alpine and inner-European zone the ethnic names (Norici, Vindelici, Brigantii, Ceutrones, Veragri, Raeti, Boii, Eravisci) likewise derive from later Greco-Roman sources (Strabo, Caesar, Pliny, Ptolemy). Many sites below are known only archaeologically and are unnamed in the texts; their historicalName is a modern site name or a later toponym, flagged in each record. Inner Germania is essentially undocumented at 278 BCE; no Germanic town has been invented. Confirming Pleiades ids and site coordinates manually remains an integration prerequisite.
politicalContext278Bce: At 278 BCE Britain, Ireland and much of non-Mediterranean Europe lie outside the literate Mediterranean record. Britain and Ireland are known almost solely through archaeology and through Pytheas of Massalia (c. 325 BCE), whose account survives only in later quotations; their societies are Iron Age, organised around hillforts, royal/assembly sites and farming communities, with no coinage yet (British coinage begins c. 150-100 BCE) and no towns in the Mediterranean sense. In the Celtic La Tene zone of the Alps, Bohemia, Moravia and the Carpathian basin the late 4th-early 3rd c. BCE sees continued Celtic expansion, including the Gallic incursion into the Balkans and the settlement of Galatia in 278/277; the classic oppida phase does not begin in most areas until the 2nd-1st c. BCE. Inner Germania is essentially undocumented until Caesar (mid-1st c. BCE) and Ptolemy (2nd c. CE); no securely identified Germanic settlement of 278 BCE is known. No Roman province (Britannia, Germania, Raetia, Noricum, Pannonia) or medieval/Anglo-Saxon/monastic entity exists at this date.
coverageNote: This batch reaches the planning envelope (8 for region 4; 12 for region 5) only because every record is a securely identified archaeological site - a hillfort, a royal/ceremonial complex, a coastal emporion or a La Tene central place - and NOT an invented settlement. Region 4 is near-silent after Pytheas: no Iron Age British or Irish settlement in this roster has a securely attested 278 BCE place-name, and the classic British oppida (Camulodunum, Verulamium, Calleva) are later foundations that were deliberately excluded rather than retrojected onto 278. Region 5 stretches across the Alps and inner Europe: the famous Celtic oppida (Manching, Kelheim, Stradonice, Trisov, Hrazany, Stare Hradisko) are 2nd-1st c. BCE florescences, so only sites active or plausibly active in the 3rd c. BCE were admitted, and even then many are explicitly marked 'uncertain'. Inner Germania proper yields no securely identified 278 BCE settlement and is therefore not represented at all in this batch; no Germanic town has been invented. Consequently several records carry 'needs-research' readiness and debatable identity. This note documents the honest shortfall in evidence quality, not a shortfall in record count.
duplicateGuard: None of these records reproduce the active atlas sites, the deferred atlas candidates, the excluded site (Cosa), any batch-1 record (r16-ita-), or any batch-2 record (r16-gre-/r16-ana-). The id prefixes r16-bri- and r16-grm- are disjoint from all previous batches.

records.existenceEvidence: One of the largest multivallate hillforts in Britain, with a long archaeologically recorded sequence (Neolithic enclosure, Bronze Age use, major Iron Age ramparts from c. 400 BCE and occupation into the 2nd-1st c. BCE). The 278 horizon falls within its Iron Age occupation, but the settlement's precise 3rd-c. footing is inferred from excavation, not from any text.
